title: DenSparSA: A Balanced Systolic Array Approach for Dense and Sparse Matrix Multiplication
problem: Existing sparse matrix acceleration architectures incur heavy area/power overhead, undermining efficiency for dense workloads; systolic arrays excel at dense but struggle with sparse matrices.
method: DenSparSA augments classic systolic array with compact sparsity-handling circuits for unstructured sparse matrices; uses circuit gating to disable sparsity overhead during dense operations; supports both single-side and dual-side sparse multiplications.

title: Neuralink: Fast on-Device LLM Inference with Neuron Co-Activation Linking
problem: On-device LLM inference on smartphones using sparsity-based techniques (loading only active neurons from flash) suffers from excessive random I/O operations due to scattered neuron placement in flash, and smartphones face severe IOPS constraints that make these I/O patterns a critical bottleneck.
method: Neuralink reorganizes neuron placement in flash storage offline based on neuron co-activation patterns: neurons that are frequently activated together are linked contiguously in flash, enabling sequential read access that is orders of magnitude more efficient than random IOPS on mobile flash. An online stage then uses tailored data access and caching strategies aligned with the sequential layout and hardware characteristics of the target phone. The two-stage pipeline (offline co-activation profiling and layout reorganization; online cache-friendly sequential access) reduces I/O operations for sparsity-based LLM inference.

title: 11.2 A Blocker-Tolerant Receiver with VCO-Based Non-Uniform Multi-Level Time-Approximation Filter with -36dB EVM in 28nm CMOS
problem: Crowded spectrum creates out-of-band (OOB) and alias-band blockers that degrade in-band EVM after sampling. Prior time-approximation-filtering (TAF) and N-path filter designs have limited blocker rejection and reconfigurability.
method: Mixer-first receiver combining multilevel time-approximation filtering (mTAF), VCO-based integrator with embedded digitalization, and non-uniform sampling with N-path filtering. Time-gated integration patterns suppress multiple blocker types simultaneously.

title: AMD RDNA 4 Radeon 9000 Series GPU
problem: Consumer and professional GPU workloads demand higher compute throughput and power efficiency; incremental improvements on existing architectures provide limited gains.
method: RDNA 4 evolves RDNA 3 with improvements to compute units, cache hierarchy, and memory subsystem. Likely includes increased compute density, optimized for both gaming and compute workloads.

title: ARC: Warp-level Adaptive Atomic Reduction in GPUs to Accelerate Differentiable Rendering
problem: During the backward pass of rasterization-based differentiable rendering (e.g., 3D Gaussian Splatting), gradient computation requires a large volume of atomic add operations to accumulate gradients from many Gaussian primitives into shared parameters, overwhelming the atomic units in the GPU L2 cache and causing long stalls that dominate training time.
method: ARC introduces warp-level adaptive atomic reduction, a GPU microarchitecture extension that intercepts atomic add operations at the warp level before they reach the L2 cache atomic units. Within a warp, threads targeting the same memory address are first reduced together using warp-level shuffle instructions (or a small dedicated reduction buffer), producing a single atomic operation per warp instead of one per thread. The approach adaptively decides whether to apply warp-level reduction based on detected contention levels, avoiding overhead when atomics are already sparse.

title: A 16Gb 12.7Gb/s/pin LPDDR5-Ultra-Pro DRAM with 4-Phase Self-Calibration and AC-Coupled Transceiver Equalization in a 5th-Generation 10nm DRAM Process
problem: LPDDR5X speeds are approaching practical limits; demand for beyond-10.7Gb/s/pin operation motivates new transceiver techniques. High-speed DRAM channels on lossy interconnects face severe timing margin challenges requiring advanced equalization and calibration.
method: A 16Gb LPDDR5X test chip implements two key techniques: (1) 4-phase self-calibration to reduce clock phase skew further than prior methods, (2) three AC-coupled equalization schemes to enhance timing margins on lossy channels. Validation at 1.05V in 5th-gen 10nm DRAM process demonstrates 12.7Gb/s/pin operation.

title: UniZK: Accelerating Zero-Knowledge Proof with Unified Hardware and Flexible Kernel Mapping
problem: Emerging hash-function-based ZKP protocols introduce diverse computation kernels (NTT, hash functions, general polynomial arithmetic) that existing ZKP accelerators cannot efficiently support, since prior designs target only elliptic-curve-based protocols with dedicated per-kernel hardware units that waste area and underutilize resources for multi-kernel workloads.
method: UniZK uses a systolic-array-based hardware architecture enhanced with extra local links and a new vector processing mode that makes the array flexible enough to serve as a unified substrate for diverse ZKP kernels. Novel mapping strategies are developed to map NTT, hash functions, and general polynomial computations onto this unified hardware, ensuring high resource utilization without dedicated per-kernel units. Smart kernel mapping strategies handle the varied data flow and compute patterns of each primitive.

title: ClusterKV: Manipulating LLM KV Cache in Semantic Space for Recallable Compression
problem: Long-context LLM inference (32K+ tokens) incurs massive KV cache memory costs and increased latency due to extensive memory accesses. Recent KV compression methods either permanently evict tokens (losing recall capability) or recall at coarse granularity (page/positional), degrading accuracy and output quality.
method: ClusterKV compresses KV cache by recalling tokens at semantic cluster granularity rather than permanent eviction or positional pages. Clusters tokens based on semantic similarity, implements efficient clustering, selection, indexing, and caching algorithms. Maintains a 1K–2K KV cache budget for 32K-length contexts with selective semantic-cluster-level recall.

title: UGPU: Dynamically Constructing Unbalanced GPUs for Enhanced Resource Efficiency
problem: Physical GPUs maintain a fixed, balanced ratio of compute and memory resources, which is inefficient when co-executing workloads have heterogeneous compute-to-memory demands. Partitioning a GPU into unbalanced slices requires accurate performance prediction under variable resource allocations and causes heavy data migration overhead when memory resources are redistributed.
method: UGPU dynamically carves a single physical GPU into unbalanced GPU slices—each with a tailored compute-SM count and HBM capacity—using a demand-aware resource partitioning algorithm that avoids complex analytical performance models. To handle memory redistribution without incurring the latency of traditional page migration, it introduces PageMove, which exploits the fact that all HBM memory channels share physical TSV connections within the DRAM stack, enabling parallel page migration between bank groups. PageMove pairs a customized memory address mapping with a Parallel Page Migration Mode (PPMM) and updated virtual memory management to move pages across memory dies at high throughput concurrently.

title: ADVeRL-ELF: ADVersarial ELF Malware Generation using Reinforcement Learning
problem: Deep learning malware detection models are pervasive but lack robustness analysis against adversarial attacks; Linux-based malware adversarial generation is under-investigated despite the critical importance of hardening detection systems.
method: ADVeRL-ELF uses a reinforcement learning framework to generate adversarial ELF malware by injecting semantic NOPs (no-operation instructions) within executable regions while preserving malicious functionality; the RL agent learns to place NOPs in patterns that evade detection while maintaining executable semantics.

title: Late Breaking Results: Breaking Symmetry - Unconventional Placement of Analog Circuits using Multi-Level Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
problem: Analog circuit performance is severely impacted by layout-dependent effects (LDEs); conventional symmetric placement mitigates variations but is suboptimal due to non-linear nature of LDEs, leaving performance on the table.
method: Proposes multi-level, multi-agent Q-learning framework for objective-driven analog layout optimization. Agents explore unconventional (asymmetric) placement strategies in design space using reinforcement learning. Approach is guided by functional and timing simulations to validate performance improvements. Comparison with simulated annealing baseline demonstrates RL superiority.

title: 27.2 A Voltage-Biased CMOS Hall Sensor with 1.0sµT(3σ) Offset and a 60nT/√Hz Noise-Floor
problem: Traditional current-biased Hall sensors exhibit large offset errors (tens of µT), limiting their use in precision applications like compasses and current sensors; voltage-biased architectures may offer lower offset but require novel readout design.
method: Voltage-biased Hall sensor (vs. traditional current-bias) with low-offset readout circuit in standard 0.18µm CMOS; dual arrangement outputs current rather than voltage, enabling offset cancellation and noise reduction through custom frontend design.

title: NN-AdderNet: Nonnegative and Sparse Weight Optimization Towards Ultra-Low Bitwidth AdderNet Quantization and Compression
problem: AdderNet (using sum-of-absolute-difference instead of multiplication) is efficient, but achieving low bitwidth quantization and effective model compression remains challenging, limiting deployment to resource-constrained hardware.
method: NN-AdderNet transforms the sum-of-absolute-difference (SAD) kernel to enable nonnegative weights, eliminating the need for sign bits (saving 1 bit per weight). It exploits dual-sparsity patterns in the quantized model weights for enhanced lossless compression. The method combines quantization-friendly weight transformation with sparse encoding.

title: Neo: Towards Efficient Fully Homomorphic Encryption Acceleration using Tensor Core
problem: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) imposes massive computational overhead—orders of magnitude over plaintext computation—that prevents practical deployment, while existing ASIC accelerators lack generality as FHE algorithms rapidly evolve. GPU-based solutions exist but fail to exploit tensor core (TCU) hardware for the dominant FHE primitives.
method: Neo maps the CKKS FHE scheme's core operations—Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) and polynomial multiplication—onto GPU Tensor Cores (TCUs) by reformulating them as matrix operations compatible with the TCU's INT8/FP16 matrix-multiply-accumulate pipeline. The design includes careful decomposition of NTT butterfly stages and residue number system (RNS) arithmetic to fit TCU matrix dimensions, with custom CUDA kernels orchestrating data layout, twiddle factor injection, and modular reduction to avoid overflow in low-precision arithmetic.

title: TAPAS: Thermal- and Power-Aware Scheduling for LLM Inference in Cloud Platforms
problem: LLM inference workloads exhibit fine-grained millisecond-scale phase transitions (prefill vs. decode) with distinct thermal and power profiles, which traditional cloud thermal and power management techniques are too coarse-grained to handle effectively. Cloud co-location of SaaS and IaaS workloads with differing visibility levels further complicates scheduling.
method: TAPAS is a thermal- and power-aware scheduler for LLM inference that models the per-phase (prefill/decode) thermal and power profiles of inference workloads at millisecond granularity. It leverages LLM configuration parameters (model parallelism, model size, quantization level) as scheduling knobs to trade off performance, temperature, power consumption, and output quality. The scheduler accounts for co-located SaaS and IaaS workloads, applying different control strategies depending on the level of visibility and flexibility available for each workload type.

title: Rethinking Prefetching for Intermittent Computing
problem: Conventional hardware prefetchers are energy-wasteful on batteryless energy harvesting systems (EHSs) because they aggressively fetch cache lines that are lost on power failure before any hit, wasting harvested energy. Frequent outages on EHSs mean that prefetched data that is never accessed before the next power loss represents pure energy overhead.
method: IPEX (Intermittence-aware Prefetching EXtension) is an add-on layer that wraps existing prefetchers on EHSs without replacing them. It tracks which prefetched cache blocks receive a hit before a power failure and suppresses future prefetches of lines that historically go unused ('useless prefetches'). Additionally, IPEX monitors harvested energy levels to predict imminent outages and dynamically throttles the prefetch degree at that moment, targeting only blocks likely to be accessed before power loss. The result is that harvested energy is redirected from futile prefetches toward productive forward execution progress.
